title: Build skills, not agents — decompose AI capabilities into testable, reusable components
whatItDoes: Instead of building a single large agent to handle all tasks end-to-end, decompose capabilities into small, independently testable 'skills' — each a focused function with one responsibility, such as fetching GitHub issues, running a test suite, parsing output, or writing a commit message. An orchestrator agent calls these skills in sequence, passing their outputs forward, rather than attempting the full task in one opaque loop. This pattern was developed and validated by Anthropic's own Claude Code engineering team and presented at AI Engineer World's Fair.
whatItImproves: Monolithic agent loops fail in opaque ways — a single large session compounds errors across steps and makes it impossible to isolate which action broke, turning every bug into a full-session restart. Decomposing into skills means each capability is tested in isolation before being composed into a larger workflow, so failures surface in a single testable unit, new skills can be added without touching working ones, and validated skills can be reused across engagements without rebuilding from scratch.
howToTry:
1. List the distinct capabilities your agent needs for a target task — for example: read a GitHub issue, write code to fix it, run existing tests, fix any failures, write a commit message, open a PR — and treat each as a candidate skill rather than a step inside one big prompt.
2. Implement each skill as a single, focused function, Claude Code slash command, or short standalone prompt that does exactly one thing and returns a structured result; test it in isolation with a manual run or a unit test before connecting it to anything else.
3. Write a lightweight orchestrator prompt whose only job is to call the right skill at the right time and pass its output to the next skill — keep the orchestrator's role to sequencing and decision-making, not to executing the individual steps.
4. When a skill fails, debug it in isolation without re-running the full agent; this isolation is the core payoff — failures are specific, addressable in minutes, and do not contaminate the working parts of the workflow.
5. Maintain a shared skills library for your team — document each skill's input contract, expected output, and any dependencies — so a skill validated on one project (such as a GxP-traceable commit-message generator or a validation test runner) can be dropped into a new engagement without rebuilding or retesting from scratch.
author: Barry Zhang, Mahesh Murag (Anthropic)

relevance.dailyImpact: You can reuse a skill validated on one client engagement — such as a test-runner skill that checks GxP-relevant acceptance criteria — on the next project without rebuilding it, cutting agent setup time and giving you a growing library of trusted, tested components rather than one-off scripts.
relevance.practicalBenefit: A shared team skills library with documented input-output contracts turns AI agent work into a repeatable, auditable process — each skill is a named, testable artifact you can reference in a validation package as evidence of the automated step applied during a client software delivery.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you build Claude Code agents for pharma client deliverables, a monolithic agent loop that fails mid-task forces a full restart and leaves no record of which step broke — decomposing into tested skills gives you a traceable, restartable workflow where each unit can be audited individually.

title: Add a source-lock and refusal instruction to stop the AI from going off-document
whatItDoes: A source-lock instruction tells the AI to answer only from a specific uploaded document or pasted text, and to say 'I don't know' rather than pulling from general training data when the answer isn't there. You add two lines to any prompt: one scoping the AI to your source material ('Reference only the following document') and one explicit refusal rule ('If the answer is not in this document, say so — do not use outside knowledge'). The technique works in any chat-based AI tool that accepts pasted or uploaded content.
whatItImproves: Without a source-lock, AI tools blend your uploaded document with their broader training data, producing answers that sound plausible but mix your internal SOP language with external best-practice generalisations — a failure mode that is invisible until a subject-matter expert or regulator spots the discrepancy. After adding the two-line source-lock, every answer is traceable back to the document in the prompt, and gaps in the source material surface as explicit 'not in this document' signals instead of silent hallucinations — making AI-assisted document work auditable by design.
howToTry:
1. Upload or paste the document you want the AI to work from — an SOP, validation protocol section, client brief, or procedure — into your Claude, ChatGPT, or M365 Copilot session.
2. Prefix your question with the source-lock instruction: 'Using only the document above, answer the following. If the answer is not in the document, say so — do not use outside knowledge.'
3. Ask your question (for example: 'Walk me through how to release a drawing revision' or 'What are the acceptance criteria for this test step?').
4. When the AI responds, spot-check the answer against the source: if it cites a section number or quotes a phrase, verify it exists in the document — any answer without a traceable phrase is a sign the refusal instruction was not followed and the response should be discarded.
5. For recurring tasks, save the source-lock prefix as a reusable template in your prompt library and apply it every time you need AI assistance grounded in a specific internal document rather than general knowledge.
author: Hawk Ridge Systems

relevance.dailyImpact: You can paste any validation procedure or client brief into Claude and add the source-lock prefix before asking review questions, ensuring every answer the model gives is traceable back to the document rather than drawn from general AI knowledge that may not match your client's specific standards.
relevance.practicalBenefit: AI responses produced under a source-lock instruction carry an implicit audit trail — each answer is either traceable to a named section of the input document or flagged as absent, giving you a defensible basis for including AI-assisted findings in GxP document reviews and gap analyses for pharma clients.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you use Claude or M365 Copilot to answer questions from a client's SOP or validation protocol, the model silently blends your document with its training data — a source-lock instruction forces it to stay within the document and flag gaps instead of filling them with plausible-sounding external content.

title: Use slash commands and context references in Copilot Chat to run structured code reviews without leaving VS Code
whatItDoes: GitHub Copilot Chat's built-in slash commands — /explain, /fix, /tests, /doc — combined with context references — #file, #selection, #codebase — let you run targeted, repeatable code-review steps directly inside VS Code without writing long freeform prompts. Scoping a command with a context reference (e.g. /tests #file:patients.py) locks Copilot's response to exactly the artifact you name, eliminating irrelevant suggestions from unrelated files. The commands cover the four most common review actions — understand, test, fix, and document — and can be combined in a standardised sequence that every developer on a project follows identically.
whatItImproves: Without slash commands and context references, developers write long manually scoped prompts and still receive suggestions that drift into unrelated parts of the codebase, requiring a second pass to separate useful feedback from noise. After adopting the structured command pattern each Copilot response is anchored to the specific file or selection in view, cutting the review overhead on every code change and making AI-assisted review consistent and repeatable across all contributors rather than varying by how each person phrases a freeform prompt.
howToTry:
1. Open a file in VS Code and highlight a function or block of code, then open Copilot Chat (Ctrl+Alt+I) and type /explain #selection to receive a plain-English walkthrough of exactly the highlighted code with no additional context required.
2. Type /tests #selection to generate unit tests for the selected function — Copilot proposes cases covering expected inputs, edge conditions, and error paths visible in the selection.
3. Type /fix #file:yourfile.py to ask Copilot to identify and correct issues across an entire file rather than only the current selection, useful for a final sweep before raising a pull request.
4. Type /doc #selection to generate a docstring or inline comment block for the selected function, keeping documentation in sync with code as you review.
5. Capture your standard command sequence (e.g. /explain #selection → /tests #selection → /fix #file: → /doc #selection) in a shared team wiki or CLAUDE.md equivalent as a named code-review checklist so every reviewer on the project runs the same structured steps on every GxP-relevant change.
author: GitHub

relevance.dailyImpact: You can run a consistent /explain → /tests → /fix → /doc sequence on any changed file before raising a pull request, catching logic gaps and missing test coverage in minutes without switching away from VS Code or writing a new prompt from scratch each time.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Documenting a shared slash-command review checklist for the team gives every developer and QA engineer the same AI-assisted code-review steps on every GxP-relevant change, producing consistent review coverage you can reference in validation documentation as a repeatable, named quality step applied to each commit.
relevance.whyRelevant: When reviewing code changes on a validated pharma client system, scoping each Copilot review step to a specific file or selection with a slash command means every AI suggestion is anchored to the exact artifact under review rather than drifting across the codebase and generating noise that slows down a compliance-sensitive code review.

title: Map every reasoning branch before you commit — Tree of Thoughts finds the best answer on complex decisions
whatItDoes: Tree of Thoughts (ToT) prompting instructs the model to generate and evaluate multiple distinct reasoning paths before committing to a final answer. Instead of following a single chain of thought, the model explores several possible approaches — like a decision tree — scores each branch for likely accuracy and completeness, and selects the path with the strongest logic. It is particularly effective for problems with multiple valid strategies, trade-off decisions, or situations where the first obvious approach may not be optimal.
whatItImproves: A standard chain-of-thought prompt locks the model into a single reasoning path, so if that path contains an early incorrect assumption, the entire answer is compromised. ToT catches this by exploring alternative approaches before committing, raising the quality of final answers on complex analytical tasks — such as multi-criteria risk assessments, protocol gap analyses, and vendor selection decisions — where the best answer requires systematically weighing competing options rather than following the first plausible route.
howToTry:
1. State your task, then append: 'Before answering, generate three distinct approaches to this problem. Label them Approach A, B, and C. For each, write a 2-3 sentence reasoning outline and score it 1-5 for likely accuracy and completeness.'
2. After the model scores all three approaches, follow up: 'Based on your scores, choose the strongest approach and use it to produce a complete, detailed answer.'
3. For tasks involving uncertain inputs, add a pruning step before scoring: 'Discard any approach that relies on an assumption you cannot verify from the information provided.'
4. To tighten the output, ask the model to format its approach comparison as a table — Approach, Outline, Score — before selecting the best path, so the reasoning is scannable rather than buried in prose.
5. Save the ToT instruction block as a reusable suffix in your prompt library for any task involving trade-offs, risk prioritisation, or multi-criteria analysis — it adds a short preamble of tokens and consistently improves first-draft quality on decisions where a single-path answer carries real risk.
author: Soumil Jain

relevance.dailyImpact: You can apply the ToT instruction block to any multi-criteria decision on a client engagement — comparing validation approaches, assessing vendor risk options, or reviewing competing test strategies — and receive a structured comparison of all paths before a recommendation is made, without running multiple separate prompts.
relevance.practicalBenefit: The labelled Approach A, B, C comparison the model produces before selecting an answer gives you a documented exploration of alternatives that you can include in a GxP decision-rationale log, turning an informal AI-assisted recommendation into an auditable, evidence-backed choice for a pharma client deliverable.
relevance.whyRelevant: When reviewing a complex validation protocol or selecting between multiple system design options for a pharma client, a single-path prompt commits to one approach before it has been tested against alternatives — ToT forces the model to map all viable paths first, so the one it recommends is the strongest available given the information provided.

title: Build automated M365 workflows from a plain English description — no Power Automate experience needed
whatItDoes: The Workflows Agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot lets you describe an automated task in plain English — for example, 'each weekday morning, summarise my unread emails and send the digest to my Teams channel' — and it generates and deploys a working workflow connecting Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and Planner without you writing a single connector rule. The agent configures the trigger, the AI processing step, and the actions automatically, then presents a visual designer where you can test, monitor, and adjust the result.
whatItImproves: Before the Workflows Agent, creating a recurring automation in Microsoft 365 required knowledge of Power Automate connector logic, trigger types, and action configuration — a barrier that left most employees dependent on IT or a developer to set up even simple recurring tasks. After describing the workflow in plain text, the agent handles all configuration and connects the required services, so any team member can create and own a working automation in minutes without a Power Automate licence or training.
howToTry:
1. Sign in to Microsoft Copilot at microsoft365.com or in Teams desktop, open the Agents panel in the left navigation, and add the Workflows Agent (Frontier) from the Agent Store — the agent is available to Microsoft 365 Personal, Family, and Premium plans in the Frontier early-access programme.
2. Select the Workflows Agent and type a plain-English description of the automation you want — for example: 'Every weekday morning, check my Outlook inbox for unread emails from the last 24 hours, identify anything high-priority or time-sensitive, and post a summary to my Teams chat organised into Needs Response, For Your Information, and Other.'
3. Review the workflow the agent generates in the Workflow tab, checking the trigger, the AI prompt step, and the output action to confirm the services connected match your intent.
4. Select Test to run the workflow once and review the output in the Activity tab — confirm the summary arrives in Teams with the expected sections and that the sender, subject, and next steps are captured correctly.
5. When satisfied, save and turn the workflow on; monitor all runs from the Activity page and refine the natural-language description at any time to adjust what the agent filters, how it labels sections, or where it sends output.
author: Microsoft

relevance.dailyImpact: You can set up a workflow that monitors your Outlook inbox for pharma client project updates overnight and delivers a prioritised summary to your Teams chat each morning, cutting the time you spend triaging email before your first client call and ensuring time-sensitive validation queries are never missed.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Automating recurring status-check and notification steps — such as alerting the team when a SharePoint validation document is updated or posting a daily summary of open Planner tasks to a project channel — removes manual monitoring overhead from client engagement workflows and creates a lightweight audit trail of communication activity across a GxP project.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you manage recurring information-gathering tasks across Microsoft 365 — triaging project emails, monitoring SharePoint document updates, or tracking open Planner tasks — the Workflows Agent lets you automate the collection and digest step without raising a ticket with IT or learning Power Automate connector logic.

title: Enable Claude's extended thinking mode for complex analysis — deeper reasoning, fewer missed steps
whatItDoes: Extended thinking is a reasoning mode in Claude (available on Fable-class models and above) that allocates a dedicated token budget for the model to reason privately before writing its answer. When enabled, Claude explores multiple approaches, checks its own logic, and resolves contradictions in an internal scratchpad that runs before the visible response — producing more accurate outputs on multi-step analytical tasks without any change to the prompt itself.
whatItImproves: Without extended thinking, Claude commits to an answer in a single forward pass, meaning logical gaps and missed edge cases only surface during your review of the output. With extended thinking on, the model catches those gaps before it answers — raising first-draft accuracy on complex tasks and reducing the number of follow-up correction rounds needed to reach a usable result.
howToTry:
1. In Claude.ai, open a conversation, click the model selector, choose a Fable-class or higher model, and toggle 'Extended thinking' on before sending your query — no change to your prompt is required.
2. Send a genuinely complex task: reviewing a multi-section validation protocol for logical gaps, assessing regulatory risk across several criteria simultaneously, or reasoning through a multi-step data inconsistency in a client dataset.
3. Read the collapsible 'Thinking' block that appears above the answer — it shows the reasoning steps Claude took; scan it to verify the logic before using the final output.
4. Via the API, add {"thinking": {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 8000}} to your request parameters; increase budget_tokens (up to the model's documented maximum) for the most demanding tasks.
5. Reserve extended thinking for tasks where missing an edge case has real consequences — for routine drafting or simple queries, keep it off to avoid unnecessary token cost.
author: Anthropic

relevance.dailyImpact: You can toggle extended thinking on in Claude.ai before any demanding document review task and receive a more thorough, self-audited response without writing a longer or more complex prompt.
relevance.practicalBenefit: The visible thinking block returned with each extended-thinking response gives you a reviewable reasoning trace you can screenshot and include in a review log as documented evidence of the analytical steps behind an AI-assisted conclusion in a GxP-adjacent deliverable.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you use Claude to review a complex validation protocol, assess cross-referenced regulatory requirements, or reason through a multi-step GxP data problem for a pharma client, a single-pass response risks missing logical dependencies that extended thinking catches internally before the answer is written.

title: Replace VLOOKUP and pivot tables with plain English questions in Excel using Copilot
whatItDoes: Copilot in Excel lets you query, summarize, and visualize tabular data using plain English questions typed into a side panel, without writing formulas, creating pivot tables, or knowing Excel functions. You describe what you want — 'show me the top 10 rows by total value' or 'highlight all rows where the status is Overdue' — and Copilot generates the formula, conditional format, or chart, explains what it will do, and applies it directly to your sheet. The feature works on any formatted Excel table and is available to all Microsoft 365 Copilot subscribers.
whatItImproves: Before Copilot in Excel, non-technical team members had to ask a developer or analyst to answer ad hoc data questions, or invest time learning VLOOKUP, SUMIF, and pivot table syntax to get answers themselves. After enabling Copilot, anyone who can describe a question in plain English can get the answer directly from the spreadsheet in seconds — removing the dependency on a technical colleague and the turnaround delay on every data request.
howToTry:
1. Open an Excel workbook containing your data and format it as a table: select any cell in the data range, press Ctrl+T, and confirm the range so Copilot can read its structure.
2. Click the Copilot button in the Home ribbon (requires a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence) to open the Copilot side panel.
3. Type a plain English question about your data — for example: 'What are the top 5 items by total value?' or 'Highlight all rows where the Status column says Overdue.'
4. Review Copilot's explanation of what it will do before clicking Apply to let it insert the formula, conditional format, or chart into your sheet.
5. If the result needs adjustment, refine your question in plain English — for example, 'Now group those results by month and show them as a bar chart' — without editing any formula directly.
author: Microsoft Excel Team

relevance.dailyImpact: You can open any formatted Excel sheet — a test case log, a validation milestone tracker, or a client project dashboard — and ask Copilot to surface overdue items, summarize completion rates, or highlight gaps without touching a formula or constructing a pivot table.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Replacing manual formula work with plain English queries on recurring Excel deliverables such as validation status reports and client project dashboards cuts the time spent on data summarization and eliminates formula errors in documents reviewed by pharma clients.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you need to answer a quick data question from a pharma client's validation status tracker or project delivery spreadsheet, Copilot in Excel lets you get the answer by describing it in plain English rather than waiting for a developer or building a formula yourself.

title: Use CHANGELOG.md and the Ralph loop to keep Claude Code on task across multi-session builds
whatItDoes: Two complementary techniques for long-running Claude Code sessions: a CHANGELOG.md progress file that acts as the agent's portable memory across sessions — recording completed tasks, failed approaches, and checkpoint results — and the Ralph loop, a scaffolding command that automatically re-prompts Claude Code when it falsely declares a complex task complete before the real acceptance criteria are met. Both are encoded in the project's CLAUDE.md so they apply automatically on every session start.
whatItImproves: Without a progress file, each new session re-discovers dead ends and duplicates work from prior sessions, losing hours on approaches already proven wrong. Without the Ralph loop, multi-step builds stop prematurely when Claude reports done but the task is not yet at spec — a failure mode that only surfaces on manual review. Together these patterns reduce wasted session restarts and keep autonomous builds converging toward their completion criteria across days of unattended work.
howToTry:
1. Create a CLAUDE.md at the repo root containing the project plan, acceptance criteria, and an explicit instruction for Claude to maintain a CHANGELOG.md that records: current status, completed tasks, failed approaches with reasons, and test or accuracy results at key checkpoints.
2. At the start of each new session, tell Claude Code: 'Read CHANGELOG.md and pick up the next task' — this replays prior context without re-pasting it manually.
3. Install the Ralph loop plugin inside Claude Code by running /plugin install ralph-loop, or add a plain bash wrapper that re-prompts Claude every time it outputs a completion signal before the real acceptance criterion is met.
4. Invoke the loop with: /ralph-loop:ralph-loop "Keep working until [your success criterion]" --max-iterations 20 --completion-promise "DONE", replacing the criterion with a concrete, testable condition such as all existing tests passing at the required accuracy threshold.
5. Encode a Git commit instruction in CLAUDE.md — e.g. 'Commit and push after every meaningful unit of work' — so progress is recoverable if a session ends unexpectedly and the CHANGELOG.md serves as an auditable change record.
author: Siddharth Mishra-Sharma

relevance.dailyImpact: You can leave Claude Code running on a multi-file refactor or test-fix task overnight and return to a session that has continued making progress rather than stopping at the first false completion signal, cutting the number of manual check-ins needed on unattended builds.
relevance.practicalBenefit: A version-controlled CHANGELOG.md that records failed approaches and checkpoint results gives you an auditable log of what the agent tried and why certain paths were abandoned — a defensible artifact to include in GxP validation documentation when AI assistance contributed to a software change.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you run Claude Code to build or refactor a validated software component across multiple sessions for a pharma client, lost progress and premature task completion are the two most common failure modes — CHANGELOG.md and the Ralph loop directly eliminate both.

title: List what you don't want the AI to write — negative constraints cut more rework than positive instructions
whatItDoes: Negative constraint prompting adds an explicit 'Do not:' section to any prompt, listing phrasing, structures, or vocabulary the model must avoid — banned opening words, forbidden filler terms, disallowed rhetorical patterns, or length ceilings. Where positive instructions tell the model what to include, negative constraints eliminate specific failure modes before the first word is generated, narrowing the model's output space to responses that already meet your quality bar. The technique is distinct from asking for a style (e.g. 'be concise') because it targets concrete, testable tokens rather than leaving interpretation to the model.
whatItImproves: Without negative constraints, the same prompt reliably produces the same recurring flaws — generic openers, junk filler phrases, or structures that require manual cleanup on every pass. After adding a compact 'Do not:' block, those failure modes disappear from the first draft, removing a systematic editing step from every AI-assisted writing task and making outputs closer to submission-ready without an extra correction round.
howToTry:
1. Run a prompt you use regularly and note two or three specific things in the output that consistently require editing — a filler opener, a banned word, an unwanted structure, or excessive length.
2. Add a 'Do not:' block at the end of your prompt. List each failure mode as a concrete, testable rule — for example: 'Do not start with In today's, In the world of, or Whether you are' rather than 'Be concise.'
3. Ban vocabulary classes rather than requesting a style — 'Do not use the words: leverage, streamline, delve, unlock, or transform' outperforms 'Write simply' because it eliminates specific tokens the model can test against.
4. Test: run the same task with and without your 'Do not:' block and compare first-draft quality — the gain is most visible on writing tasks you run repeatedly.
5. Build a reusable 'Do not:' block for each recurring deliverable type — client status update, validation finding summary, executive brief — and add it to your saved prompt templates so the constraint applies automatically every session.
author: Amara

relevance.dailyImpact: You can add a five-line 'Do not:' block to any recurring prompt template and stop manually editing out the same filler phrases, generic openers, and overused vocabulary from every AI-assisted deliverable in your weekly workflow.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Encoding negative constraints in shared prompt templates for GxP document reviews and client deliverables gives every team member the same quality floor on first drafts, reducing per-document cleanup time across the engagement and making AI-assisted output consistently closer to submission-ready.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you use Claude or M365 Copilot to draft client status updates or validation finding summaries, the same junk phrases and generic openers appear every time because nothing in your prompt eliminates them — a negative constraint block removes those specific failure modes before the first draft is generated.

title: Add a copilot-instructions.md file so GitHub Copilot learns your project rules automatically
whatItDoes: A .github/copilot-instructions.md file in any repository gives GitHub Copilot standing project-specific context — coding conventions, test frameworks, naming patterns, GxP documentation requirements, and restricted modules — that applies automatically to every inline suggestion and Copilot Chat response in that repo without re-stating it each session. The file is plain Markdown and is read by GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Visual Studio, and JetBrains IDEs with no plugin or settings change required.
whatItImproves: Without a custom instructions file, every developer re-explains the same project conventions in Copilot Chat at the start of each session, producing inconsistent AI suggestions across the team. After adding the file, Copilot applies the same standing context to every suggestion automatically — removing the per-session re-briefing step and making AI assistance consistent across all contributors on a shared project.
howToTry:
1. Create a .github folder at the root of your repository if one does not already exist.
2. Add a file named copilot-instructions.md inside that folder.
3. Write your project conventions in plain Markdown — for example: test naming pattern (test_<method>_when_<scenario>), required GxP-traceable comment format for each change, dependency injection style, and any modules the AI must not modify.
4. Commit and push the file; GitHub Copilot picks it up immediately in VS Code with no extension update or additional configuration required.
5. Open Copilot Chat and ask a project-specific question to verify — the response should reflect your stated conventions without you having to mention them.
author: GitHub

relevance.dailyImpact: You open VS Code on a client project and GitHub Copilot already knows the test framework, naming patterns, and GxP documentation requirements encoded in the repo's copilot-instructions.md, so every suggestion and chat response is aligned from the first keystroke without any per-session setup.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Encoding GxP-traceable comment requirements and restricted module rules in a shared, version-controlled copilot-instructions.md gives your pharma client an auditable record of the AI assistance conventions applied consistently across their validated codebase.
relevance.whyRelevant: When multiple i2e developers work on the same validated software project, each person currently re-explains GxP comment standards, test naming conventions, and restricted module rules in separate Copilot Chat sessions — producing inconsistent AI assistance across the team on every pharma client engagement.

title: Use two or three worked examples instead of instructions to get consistent AI output every time
whatItDoes: Few-shot prompting supplies the AI with two or three concrete input-output examples before stating the actual task, letting the model pattern-match a visible template rather than interpret a written description. The examples teach format, tone, field names, and edge-case handling simultaneously — information that instructions alone rarely convey with enough precision. Three deliberately varied examples covering a normal case, a borderline case, and a near-miss edge case outperform a longer instruction block on every repeated, structured task.
whatItImproves: Without examples, the same prompt produces differently structured responses on every run, forcing manual cleanup before the output can be used in a deliverable, review log, or shared template. After adding a small example set, the model locks onto the demonstrated pattern and reproduces it reliably across different inputs — removing the reformatting step and making the output ready to insert directly into a document or pass to a downstream step without post-processing.
howToTry:
1. Pick a task you run repeatedly — for example, summarising a validation finding, writing a client status bullet, or flagging a test-script gap — and collect two or three outputs you already consider correct.
2. Format each as an explicit Example block: Input: [the raw text] → Output: [the structured result you want], matching the exact headings, field names, and length you expect.
3. Include at least one example that shows a tricky or borderline case — an input with missing data, an ambiguous phrasing, or an edge condition the model is likely to encounter — so it learns how to handle the hard cases, not just the easy ones.
4. Paste all examples above the live task in your prompt, then add: 'Now apply the same format to the following input:' followed by the real content.
5. Test the prompt on three different inputs and check whether the output structure is identical each time; if a field drifts or disappears, replace the weakest example with one that demonstrates the expected behaviour for that field.

relevance.dailyImpact: You can build a three-example few-shot block once for each recurring deliverable type — validation finding summary, gap-analysis row, client status bullet — paste it at the top of your prompt, and receive consistently formatted output across every session without manual cleanup.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Standardising a shared few-shot block for GxP document reviews means every team member gets the same field names, heading order, and length constraints in their AI output regardless of how they word the rest of the prompt, reducing individual variation and making AI-assisted drafts audit-ready from the first pass.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you use Claude or M365 Copilot to extract findings from a validation protocol or produce a structured client status update, a written description of the format you want is rarely precise enough — two worked examples using your own document style give the model an exact template to copy rather than approximate.

title: Work through multi-step problems with the ReAct loop — Thought, Action, Observation, repeat
whatItDoes: ReAct (Reason + Act) is a prompting pattern that instructs the model to cycle through three explicitly labelled steps — THOUGHT (what should I do next?), ACTION (take that step), and OBSERVATION (what did I learn from it?) — repeating the loop until a task is fully resolved. Unlike chain-of-thought, which produces a single linear reasoning trace and then stops, ReAct treats each step as a checkpoint that can change direction based on what the previous action revealed, making it suited to multi-step analytical, research, and review tasks.
whatItImproves: Without ReAct, complex tasks collapse into a single unguided response that commits to an approach before testing it, so gaps and wrong assumptions only surface after the final answer is already written. After applying the ReAct pattern the model self-corrects mid-task: each OBSERVATION feeds the next THOUGHT, so missing information or a flawed assumption is caught inside the loop rather than surfacing in a client review of the finished deliverable.
howToTry:
1. Add the ReAct instruction at the end of your prompt: 'Work through this step by step. For each step, label it THOUGHT (what you should do next), ACTION (do it), and OBSERVATION (what you learned). Repeat until you have a complete, verified answer.'
2. Give the model a multi-step analytical task — for example, reviewing a validation protocol section for gaps, checking a client data report for inconsistencies, or building a risk register from a project brief.
3. Read each OBSERVATION before the model moves on. If an observation misses a relevant condition, prompt it: 'Continue from your last OBSERVATION and also check [specific aspect] before proceeding.'
4. Once all loops are complete, ask for a synthesis: 'Summarise your findings from all THOUGHT-ACTION-OBSERVATION cycles into a single structured output in [format].'
5. Save the ReAct instruction as a standard suffix in your prompt library for any task that requires checking multiple conditions or sources — it adds negligible tokens and consistently improves completeness on analytical work.
author: Pasquale Pillitteri

relevance.dailyImpact: You can apply the ReAct loop to any multi-condition document review — such as checking a test script for logical gaps or cross-referencing a client brief against project requirements — and get a structured trace of every reasoning step rather than a single summary that may have skipped something.
relevance.practicalBenefit: ReAct's labelled THOUGHT-ACTION-OBSERVATION steps produce an auditable reasoning trace you can include in a review log, giving you documented evidence of the checks performed during an AI-assisted validation step on a pharma client deliverable.
relevance.whyRelevant: When reviewing a validation protocol or performing a GxP-aware data check, a single-pass prompt misses edge cases that a ReAct loop catches by forcing the model to observe what it found before deciding what to check next.

title: Add a self-evaluation step so the model critiques and rewrites its own output before you read it
whatItDoes: Instead of accepting a first-draft AI response, you append a structured critique-and-revise instruction asking the model to score its own output against explicit quality criteria — accuracy, completeness, appropriate length, absence of unsupported claims — and then rewrite any section that falls short. The technique turns a single prompt into a two-stage loop: generate, then self-evaluate, then refine. It works in one combined prompt or as a two-call chain where the second call receives the first output as input.
whatItImproves: Without a self-evaluation step, the first AI response is treated as final even when it contains gaps, inconsistencies, or sections that fail the delivery standard — and those gaps only surface during your manual review round. Adding the critique step moves that discovery upstream: the model flags and fixes its own weaknesses before you read the output, raising first-draft quality and cutting the back-and-forth correction cycles that slow document delivery work.
howToTry:
1. Write your task prompt as normal and get a first response from Claude, ChatGPT, or Copilot.
2. Send a follow-up instruction — or append it to the original prompt — using this pattern: 'Now evaluate your response against these criteria: [list your criteria, e.g. factual accuracy, completeness against the source, no unsupported claims, consistent terminology, appropriate length]. Score each criterion 1–5 and list any specific gap.'
3. Send a third instruction: 'Rewrite only the sections that scored below 4, correcting the identified gaps without changing sections that passed.'
4. For recurring deliverables, embed all three stages in a single system prompt or saved prompt template so the loop runs automatically on every use.
5. Tune the criteria list to your delivery standard — for GxP validation documents, add criteria such as 'no claim made without a traceable source in the input document' and 'terminology matches the input protocol exactly'.

relevance.dailyImpact: You can embed a self-evaluation step into your standard validation document review prompt so Claude flags incomplete sections, inconsistent terminology, or unsupported assertions before you read the output, cutting the time you spend on a first-pass review of each GxP deliverable.
relevance.practicalBenefit: A reusable self-evaluation prompt template applied to recurring client deliverables — gap analyses, validation summaries, status reports — produces consistently higher-quality first drafts that require fewer correction rounds before submission, reducing revision time per document across the engagement.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you use Claude or ChatGPT to draft validation protocols or client deliverables, a model that self-critiques against your specific quality criteria catches gaps in completeness and unsupported claims before you do — removing a manual review round from every AI-assisted document session.

title: Load every client SOP and standing rule into a Claude Project — brief it once, never again
whatItDoes: Claude Projects creates a named workspace that permanently stores a custom system prompt, uploaded reference files, and the full conversation history from every session inside it. Any document you upload — SOPs, validation templates, protocol excerpts, client briefing notes — remains available to Claude in every future session without being pasted again. The system prompt persists automatically, so your role definition, output format rules, and standing instructions apply from the very first message every time you open that project.
whatItImproves: Without Projects, every Claude session starts blank: you re-paste context, re-upload documents, and re-explain your role before any real work can begin, adding several minutes of overhead to every session. With a Project in place, that ramp-up drops to zero — Claude already knows the engagement context, the document set, and the required output style from the first message, and every team member who opens the same project gets the same consistently briefed starting point.
howToTry:
1. Open Claude at claude.ai, click 'Projects' in the left sidebar, then select 'New Project' and give it a client or engagement name.
2. Click 'Set project instructions' and write a system prompt covering your role, the client context, standing output rules, and audience — for example: 'You are assisting a GxP validation consultant at i2e. Format all findings in two sections: Gaps and Recommendations. Use plain language suitable for a QA manager.'
3. Click 'Add content' to upload reference files — SOPs, validation plan templates, protocol excerpts, client briefing documents — that Claude should draw on across all sessions in this project.
4. Open any new conversation inside the project; Claude automatically applies your system instructions and has access to all uploaded files from the first message, with no re-briefing needed.
5. Update the project instructions or replace uploaded files whenever the engagement scope changes — the updated context applies immediately to all subsequent sessions.
author: Anthropic

relevance.dailyImpact: You can open a Project pre-loaded with your client's validation templates and standing output instructions and start a document review or gap-analysis session from the first message, with no setup overhead on any return visit.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Uploading GxP reference documents and a project-specific system prompt gives your entire engagement team a shared, consistently briefed AI workspace — so every consultant produces outputs in the same format and draws on the same reference material without maintaining a separate shared-prompt document.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you work on a recurring pharma client engagement using Claude, re-pasting the same project context, SOPs, and role instructions at the start of every session wastes time that a Claude Project eliminates entirely.

title: Pin down the output format before the model writes anything
whatItDoes: Structured output prompting means telling the model exactly what shape its response must take — headers, JSON fields, table columns, numbered lists, or a fixed schema — before it writes a single word of content. Instead of asking for 'a summary', you supply the precise structure: field names, order, length limits, and any mandatory sections. The model then fills that skeleton rather than inventing its own layout.
whatItImproves: Without a declared output format, the same prompt produces differently structured responses on every run — forcing a manual cleanup step to standardise fields, headings, or delimiters before the output can be used in a document, a downstream system, or a shared template. After adding an explicit format block, output structure becomes stable and predictable across runs, removing the reformatting step entirely and making AI-generated content drop directly into review workflows or parsed by code without post-processing.
howToTry:
1. Decide the exact structure you need: a JSON object with named fields, a markdown table with fixed columns, a numbered list with a header per item, or a two-section report (Findings / Recommendations). Write it down before you write the prompt.
2. Add a Format section at the end of your prompt — after the task instruction — that shows the skeleton: for JSON, list every key; for a table, name every column; for a report, name every heading and specify the maximum word count per section.
3. For structured data (JSON, CSV), include one example row with placeholder values so the model can copy the exact format rather than approximating it.
4. If you need the model to reason before it formats, add: 'Work through the problem first, then return only the result in the format below.' This preserves chain-of-thought internally while keeping the output clean.
5. Run the same prompt three times on different inputs and check whether the structure is identical each time; if a field drifts or disappears, tighten the format instruction by making that field mandatory with a fallback value such as N/A.
author: Rizki Murtadha

relevance.dailyImpact: You can define a two-section Findings/Recommendations skeleton in your prompt and receive consistently structured output across every document review session, cutting the time you spend rearranging AI responses before they are ready for a colleague or a pharma client to review.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Locking the output format in shared prompt templates for GxP document reviews, gap analyses, and client deliverables means every team member receives the same structured result regardless of how they word the rest of the prompt — reducing individual variation and making AI-assisted drafts audit-ready from the first pass.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you use Claude or ChatGPT to extract findings from a validation protocol or draft a structured client status update, an undeclared output format means every response looks different — structured output prompting gives you the same field layout every time, so the result slots directly into your Word template or review checklist without manual reformatting.

title: Fix silent AI agent failures by managing context across seven layers
whatItDoes: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what information enters an AI agent's context window, when it gets there, and in what form — spanning seven distinct layers: system prompt, user input, retrieved knowledge, tool outputs, conversation history, structured intermediate outputs, and persistent memory. Unlike prompt engineering, which optimises a single message, context engineering manages the entire information architecture across a multi-step session. Production agent failures today are almost always context failures — wrong documents, stale memory, contradictory instructions, or conversation history that crowds out critical earlier guidance.
whatItImproves: Before applying context engineering, agent sessions degrade silently: a hallucination in one turn becomes a stated fact in the next (context poisoning), or irrelevant detail high in the window pulls model attention away from critical instructions (context distraction). After structuring each of the seven layers deliberately — placing instructions at window edges, compressing old history before new tool outputs, and loading retrieved documents on-demand rather than upfront — agent accuracy stabilises across long sessions and token costs drop because the window carries only what the current step needs.
howToTry:
1. Map your agent's seven context layers: write down what fills each one in your current setup — system prompt, user input, retrieved chunks, tool outputs, prior turns, intermediate results, and memory — and flag which layer is largest and least controlled.
2. Fix information ordering first: place your most critical instructions at the very start and very end of the context window; the 'lost in the middle' effect means accuracy on information buried in a long window drops measurably compared to content at the edges.
3. Compress conversation history before it crowds instructions: summarise turns older than five exchanges into a short paragraph and replace the raw turn-by-turn record with that summary, keeping the window lean for new tool outputs.
4. Switch from static to on-demand retrieval: instead of injecting your full knowledge base at session start, retrieve only the chunks relevant to the current step and add them just before the model call — this reserves token budget for tool outputs that arrive mid-loop.
5. Identify your dominant failure mode after each session — context poisoning, context distraction, context confusion, or context clash — and address the specific layer that caused it rather than rewriting the prompt.
author: Samira Qureshi

relevance.dailyImpact: Applying on-demand retrieval and conversation-history compression to any recurring agent session you run for pharma deliverables cuts both the token cost per session and the frequency of mid-task hallucinations that require you to restart from scratch.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Structuring your agent's context window using the seven-layer framework gives you a concrete, auditable configuration you can document in a GxP validation package — turning an informal 'we use Claude' statement into a specified, repeatable information architecture.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you run Claude or ChatGPT agents across multi-step validation document reviews, the failures you see — wrong section referenced, contradictory guidance, cost spikes — are almost always context failures that a structured seven-layer approach directly fixes.

title: Wrap prompt sections in XML tags to stop Claude misreading your instructions
whatItDoes: When a prompt contains multiple logical sections — instructions, background context, a reference document, examples, and output constraints — wrapping each in named XML tags (e.g., <context>, <document>, <task>, <examples>, <format>) tells the model exactly where each section starts and ends. Claude is specifically trained to parse XML-tagged sections; the pattern also improves boundary clarity on GPT-5.6 and Gemini. Without tags, the model must infer boundaries from whitespace and prose transitions, which regularly causes it to apply instructions to the wrong block of text.
whatItImproves: Before XML tagging, long multi-section prompts caused models to blend instructions with reference material or ignore example blocks entirely, forcing two or three refinement rounds to correct misaligned output. After adopting XML structure, the model reads each section cleanly and in isolation, cutting the average number of follow-up corrections needed to reach a usable result — the gain is sharpest on prompts that mix a large reference document with precise instructions and a specific output format.
howToTry:
1. Identify the logical sections in your prompt: persona or role, background context, the reference document or data the model should draw from, the task itself, any examples, and the required output format.
2. Wrap each section in descriptive XML tags — for example: <context>...</context>, <document>...</document>, <task>...</task>, <examples>...</examples>, <format>...</format>.
3. Order the sections so the <task> block appears last, after all supporting material, so the instruction is freshest in the model's attention when it starts generating.
4. For Claude specifically, pre-fill the opening of the Assistant turn with the first tag or word of the expected output (e.g., <output>) to anchor the response structure and prevent the model from adding unsolicited preamble.
5. Run the same prompt with and without XML tags on any multi-section task and compare output quality; the difference is most visible on prompts longer than 400 words that mix reference text with instructions.
author: Nadia Dubois

relevance.dailyImpact: You can wrap any validation protocol section in <document> tags and your review criteria in <task> tags so Claude applies its reasoning to the correct content block without needing a clarifying follow-up, saving at least one prompt-correction round on every document review session.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Embedding XML-tagged sections in shared prompt templates for client deliverables and GxP document reviews gives every team member a portable, reusable structure that produces consistent, predictable outputs across repeated uses — reducing individual variation in AI-assisted draft quality.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you send Claude a prompt that mixes a validation document excerpt, review instructions, and an output format requirement, XML tags prevent the model from treating your reference text as instructions — a boundary error that produces off-target outputs on multi-section pharma deliverables.

title: Run multi-file edits and test-fix loops with GitHub Copilot Agent Mode
whatItDoes: GitHub Copilot Agent Mode lets you describe a task at the goal level — not the file level — and have the agent plan the steps, edit multiple files, run terminal commands, read error output, and iterate until the task is done, all without you directing each step manually. It operates inside VS Code, reads your full workspace context automatically, and since mid-2026 supports MCP servers so the agent can query external systems like databases directly during a task.
whatItImproves: Before agent mode, AI coding assistance required you to specify which files to open and what exactly to change, then manually apply diffs and re-run tests yourself. After enabling agent mode, you hand off a task with acceptance criteria and the agent closes the edit-run-fix loop autonomously — the biggest gain is on test-fix cycles where terminal output feeds directly back into code corrections without any manual copy-paste.
howToTry:
1. Install VS Code 1.99+, ensure the GitHub Copilot Chat extension is installed, and add these settings: {"github.copilot.chat.agent.enabled": true, "github.copilot.chat.agent.runTasks": true, "github.copilot.chat.agent.autoFix": true}.
2. Open the Copilot Chat panel (Ctrl+Alt+I) and switch the dropdown at the top to Agent mode.
3. Write a task with clear acceptance criteria and explicit scope constraints — e.g. "Add input validation to the POST /patients endpoint. Only change files in src/routes/ and src/middleware/. Run the existing tests and fix any failures."
4. Read the agent's plan before it starts; if the approach or files look wrong, reject it and refine the prompt before the agent touches anything.
5. Review the resulting diffs in the Source Control panel; accept, reject, or ask the agent to adjust specific parts before committing.
author: Carlos Oliva Pascual

relevance.dailyImpact: You can hand the agent a failing test suite and a task description and then review the final diff rather than driving each edit step yourself, freeing your attention for checking the output for GxP compliance instead of mechanics.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Agent mode's autonomous test-fix loop produces cleaner, test-passing commits with less back-and-forth debugging, giving you stronger audit evidence to include in client delivery reviews and validation packages.
relevance.whyRelevant: When building or validating software features for pharma clients, agent mode lets you describe a multi-file change and its acceptance criteria once and have the agent close the edit-test-fix loop, cutting the manual file-by-file iteration that slows delivery against tight project timelines.

title: Turn a Copilot chat into a shareable, editable document with Copilot Pages
whatItDoes: Copilot Pages splits the M365 Copilot interface into a chat window and a live document canvas, letting you turn any AI response into a persistent, editable page without leaving the chat. You can keep prompting Copilot to add or rewrite sections of the page, edit text directly on the canvas, and share the live page with colleagues as a Loop component embedded in Teams, Outlook, or Word. No separate Copilot licence is required — the feature is available to any Microsoft 365 subscriber with SharePoint or OneDrive storage.
whatItImproves: Before Copilot Pages, AI-generated output had to be manually copied into Word or another editor, losing the live connection with Copilot and requiring separate sharing steps. With Pages, the document stays live beside the chat — Copilot can keep refining it on request, collaborators can edit it in real time, and the finished page exports directly to Word or PowerPoint, collapsing a multi-step copy-paste-share cycle into a single session.
howToTry:
1. Open microsoft365.com and start a Copilot Chat session; prompt Copilot for any work output such as a meeting agenda, project outline, or gap-analysis list.
2. When the response looks useful, click the pencil (Edit in Pages) icon at the bottom of the result to open it as a page beside the chat.
3. Edit the page text directly and continue prompting Copilot in the left window; use the Copilot shortcuts icon at the lower-right to adjust tone, add an introduction, or make the whole page more concise.
4. Click the Share icon at the upper-right of the page, then copy either the page link or the Loop component link and paste it into a Teams chat or Outlook email — recipients can edit in real time without seeing your chat history.
5. When the page is final, export it to Word or PowerPoint via the page menu for client-ready formatting.
author: Howard Wen

relevance.dailyImpact: You can share a Copilot Page as a Loop component in a Teams chat or Outlook email so colleagues edit it in real time, cutting the rounds of email-attachment back-and-forth that slow down collaborative document reviews on pharma deliverables.
relevance.practicalBenefit: The export-to-Word step means your AI-assisted draft ends up in the format pharma clients expect for validation deliverables, with all manual edits and Copilot refinements captured in one session rather than spread across tools.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you use M365 Copilot to draft a validation summary or client status update, Copilot Pages lets you refine that output in a live document beside the chat instead of copying it into Word and losing the AI connection.

title: Version your prompts like code — stop silent regressions in AI-assisted workflows
whatItDoes: Prompt versioning treats every prompt as an immutable, versioned artifact with a unique content-addressable ID — storing not just the text but the temperature setting, model hash, and expected input variables in a centralized registry. Any change to a prompt creates a new version rather than silently overwriting the old one, giving teams a rollback path and a complete audit trail of exactly what the model was asked at any point in time. Schema validation gates each new version, blocking a rollout automatically if the new prompt would break the structure downstream parsers expect.
whatItImproves: Before prompt versioning, small uncoordinated edits by different team members silently degraded AI output quality with no way to pinpoint when or why — a pattern called prompt drift. After adopting a versioned registry, every regression is traceable to a specific version diff, rollback takes seconds, and quality metrics are tied to exact prompt IDs so teams can measure which version actually performs better instead of relying on gut feel.
howToTry:
1. Move all prompt templates out of application code and into a centralized registry (Git-based for developer-heavy teams, or a proxy-based platform such as Braintrust or Agenta for non-technical collaborators who need instant updates without a redeploy).
2. Assign each prompt a content-addressable ID — a hash of the full prompt text plus its configuration parameters (model, temperature, top-p, input variable names) — so identical content always produces the same ID and changes are always detectable.
3. Add schema validation: before any version is tagged 'production', run a small set of few-shot tests confirming the model still returns correctly structured output and block the rollout automatically if the schema breaks.
4. Tag every live request with its prompt version ID and pipe those tags into your analytics or logging tool so you can build per-version quality heatmaps and catch regressions before users do.
5. For multi-step agent chains, version the entire bundle of prompts as a tested unit rather than individual prompts in isolation, and use canary rollouts to validate aggregate chain behavior before full promotion.
author: Mohamed Ali

relevance.dailyImpact: If a prompt used in a recurring client deliverable — such as a protocol gap-analysis template — produces unexpected output after someone edited it, you can roll back to the last known-good version in seconds rather than trying to reconstruct the previous wording from memory.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Version-linked quality metrics let you demonstrate to a pharma client that a specific, immutable prompt configuration was used consistently throughout a validation cycle, turning what was informal configuration into a traceable, auditable artifact alongside the rest of your delivery evidence.
relevance.whyRelevant: When your team uses Claude or ChatGPT prompts to drive validation document reviews or GxP-aware data steps, any untracked wording change can silently degrade output quality in a way that only surfaces during a client review — prompt versioning gives you an auditable record of exactly what the model was asked at each point in the project.

title: Separate static and dynamic context to cut AI agent costs by up to 90%
whatItDoes: Place stable context — system instructions, tool definitions, policies, and reference documents — at the top of every prompt and keep dynamic content (user input, session data, retrieved results) below it. When the static prefix is identical across calls, the LLM provider reuses cached computation instead of reprocessing those tokens from scratch, delivering up to 90% cost reduction and up to 85% latency reduction on cache hits. A 2026 arXiv paper evaluating 500-plus long-horizon agent sessions across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google confirmed that caching a stable system context while keeping dynamic tool results out of the reusable prefix cut API costs by 41–80% and improved time-to-first-token by 13–31%.
whatItImproves: Before this separation, every prompt call reprocesses the full context from scratch — instructions, rules, and document blocks you send every single time — burning tokens you already paid for. After applying static/dynamic separation, that shared prefix is processed once and cached; only the small dynamic tail changes per call, so high-volume sessions that previously consumed tens of millions of repeated tokens per day become dramatically cheaper and faster without any change to output quality.
howToTry:
1. Identify the stable parts of your prompt: system instructions, persona definition, tool schemas, policy rules, few-shot examples, and any reference document that does not change per request.
2. Move all stable content to the very top of your prompt, before anything user-specific or session-specific.
3. Place dynamic content — user message, session ID, timestamps, retrieved results that vary per call — below the stable block.
4. Verify the static prefix is byte-for-byte identical across calls: even a single token change breaks the cache key and you lose the saving.
5. Monitor cache hit rates using your provider's token usage logs (Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google Vertex AI all report cache hits); aim for the stable prefix to account for at least 60% of total prompt tokens to see meaningful savings.
author: Emily Winks

relevance.dailyImpact: On a pharma project where an agent runs dozens of document-review queries a day against the same GxP policy context, moving that policy block into a stable cached prefix cuts both the per-call cost and the wait time for every response in the session.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Applying static/dynamic separation to any agent or automated prompt pipeline that reuses the same instructions or reference material reduces AI tooling spend by up to 90% on the cached tokens, making it practical to run more agent-assisted review cycles within the same project budget.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you build or configure Claude or ChatGPT agents that process the same validation rules, SOP snippets, or client policy documents on every call, you are paying to reprocess identical tokens repeatedly — static/dynamic separation lets the provider cache that shared prefix so you stop paying for it.

title: Cut reasoning token costs with Chain of Draft — minimal scratchpad, same accuracy
whatItDoes: Chain of Draft (CoD) is a prompting technique that instructs the model to produce extremely short intermediate reasoning steps — typically five words or fewer each — before writing its final answer. You add one sentence to your prompt: 'Think step by step, but only keep a minimum draft of each thinking step, ideally five words per step.' The model still reasons through the problem but compresses its scratchpad rather than writing out verbose chain-of-thought prose.
whatItImproves: Standard chain-of-thought prompting can multiply token usage two to five times on reasoning-heavy tasks, adding cost and latency to every analytical prompt. Chain of Draft achieves comparable accuracy while using up to 80% fewer tokens in the intermediate steps, making complex analytical prompts significantly cheaper and faster without changing the model or the underlying task.
howToTry:
1. Open Claude, ChatGPT, or M365 Copilot and write your prompt as normal.
2. Append this instruction at the end: 'Think step by step, but only keep a minimum draft of each thinking step, ideally five words per step.'
3. Run the same task with standard 'Think step by step' and compare output quality — for most reasoning and analysis tasks the results are equivalent.
4. For recurring complex tasks such as document gap analysis or data review, embed the CoD instruction in your saved prompt template or system prompt so it applies automatically.
5. If a task is highly complex and quality drops, increase the draft length slightly — try 'ten words per step' — to find the right balance between cost and thoroughness.
author: silasMartel

relevance.dailyImpact: You can add one sentence to any complex prompt and immediately reduce the token spend on every reasoning task you run on validation documents, client status write-ups, or protocol gap analyses without changing the tool or retraining your workflow.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Embedding the CoD instruction in your standard prompt templates cuts AI cost per analysis task across every project, making it easier to fit more AI-assisted document reviews and reasoning steps within a client engagement's AI budget.
relevance.whyRelevant: When running analytical or reasoning-heavy tasks in Claude — such as reviewing validation document discrepancies or checking GxP data entries — Chain of Draft gives you the same structured reasoning at up to 80% lower token cost than standard chain-of-thought.

title: Cut AI response length by 80% without losing reasoning quality using Chain of Draft
whatItDoes: Chain of Draft (CoD) is a prompting technique that instructs the AI to reason through a problem using the absolute minimum words per step — typically five words or fewer — before producing the final answer. Unlike standard Chain-of-Thought which generates verbose intermediate reasoning, CoD compresses the thinking phase into dense, minimal fragments, slashing token usage while preserving accuracy.
whatItImproves: Standard Chain-of-Thought reasoning often produces long, repetitive reasoning traces that inflate cost and latency with no benefit to output quality. Chain of Draft cuts the intermediate reasoning text by up to 80% while matching or exceeding CoT accuracy on reasoning tasks, making it practical for high-volume document drafting and review workflows where every token counts.
howToTry:
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude, or any LLM interface.
2. Add this instruction to your prompt: "Think step by step, but only keep a minimum draft for each thinking step. Each intermediate step should be at most 5 words."
3. Follow with your actual task — for example: "Think step by step, but only keep a minimum draft for each thinking step. Each intermediate step should be at most 5 words. Now review the following validation test case and identify any logical gaps: [paste content]."
4. Read the compressed reasoning trace to check the model's logic, then use the final answer.
5. Adjust the word-per-step limit (e.g. 8–10 words) if the task involves technical domain terms that need more specificity.
author: Silei Xu, Wenhao Xie, Lingxiao Zhao, Pengcheng He

relevance.dailyImpact: You can apply the five-word-step instruction to any prompt where you want the model to reason carefully — such as checking a GxP test script for logical gaps — without paying for a wall of verbose intermediate text you would skip-read anyway.
relevance.practicalBenefit: On high-volume document review tasks for pharma clients, Chain of Draft lets you keep reasoning-quality outputs at a fraction of the token cost, making AI-assisted review sustainable within project budgets without switching to a weaker model.
relevance.whyRelevant: When you use Claude or ChatGPT to review validation test cases, protocol sections, or client deliverables, adding Chain of Draft keeps the model's reasoning visible and auditable while cutting the token volume that inflates cost on repeated, high-volume tasks.

title: Let the agent interview you before any task — the /grill-me skill stops misaligned output before it starts
whatItDoes: The /grill-me skill runs a structured agent interview before any non-code task — writing, planning, analysis, or design. The agent asks targeted questions to expose gaps and assumptions before it writes a single word of output. It is the lightweight version of /grill-with-docs: no domain document required, just a conversation that turns vague intent into clear scope.
whatItImproves: The most common failure mode in AI-assisted work is misalignment — you think the agent knows what you want, then you see what it produced and realise it didn't understand you at all. With /grill-me, the communication gap closes before work begins, so the first draft is already aligned rather than needing expensive correction cycles.
howToTry:
1. Install via the Claude Code marketplace: run /plugin install mattpocock-skills inside a Claude Code session, or via CLI: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills.
2. Run /setup-matt-pocock-skills once per repo to configure your issue tracker and preferences.
3. Before any non-code task — writing, planning, analysis — type /grill-me and describe your goal in one sentence.
4. Answer the agent's questions actively: push back, add constraints, and correct assumptions. The failure mode is passivity — nodding along produces a plan the agent wrote and you rubber-stamped.
5. When the grilling ends, the agent has the context to produce a first draft that is already scoped and aligned.
author: Matt Pocock

relevance.dailyImpact: Before asking Claude to draft a GxP-compliant document or project summary, run /grill-me first; the structured interview will expose missing scope, unstated assumptions, and format preferences that would otherwise appear as feedback comments two drafts later.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Replaces the back-and-forth correction cycle that follows an under-specified prompt with a single upfront conversation — so first-draft quality is high enough to send to a colleague for review rather than revision.
relevance.whyRelevant: When kicking off a deliverable like a validation test plan, a requirements document, or a client status update, /grill-me surfaces the questions you haven't asked yourself yet — before the AI writes anything — saving the revision time that follows a vague first draft.

title: Let the AI write your prompt — meta-prompting gets better outputs by asking the model what it needs first
whatItDoes: Meta-prompting asks the model to generate the optimal prompt for your task before writing anything. You describe your goal, the model identifies the context, constraints, and examples it needs, and you use that output as the actual prompt — essentially letting the AI tell you how to ask for what you want.
whatItImproves: Before meta-prompting, crafting a good prompt required guessing what information the model needed, often producing vague outputs on the first attempt. After applying it, the model self-generates a prompt that captures the right context and constraints up front — reducing the number of refinement rounds needed to reach a usable result.
howToTry:
1. Open ChatGPT or Claude and describe your goal without writing the full prompt — e.g. "I want to create a comprehensive API documentation page for a REST API."
2. Add the meta-prompting instruction: "Before you write anything, ask me the 10 most important questions you'd need answered to create excellent documentation."
3. Answer the model's questions, then ask it to generate the optimal prompt: "Generate the optimal prompt that I should give you to get the best possible result. Include what context, constraints, and examples I should provide."
4. Use the model's generated prompt as your actual prompt for the task.
5. Optionally combine with Role + Context, Chain-of-Thought, or Constraint techniques in the generated prompt for maximum output quality.
author: HonestAI

relevance.dailyImpact: Before drafting a validation plan section or a process description for a pharma client, run a meta-prompt session first; the model's questions will surface gaps in your brief that would otherwise produce a generic first draft needing heavy revision.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Cuts the prompt-refinement cycle from three or four rounds to one by front-loading the clarification step — freeing review time for content accuracy rather than prompt iteration.
relevance.whyRelevant: When starting a new deliverable — such as a validation summary report or a client-facing status update — meta-prompting lets you ask Claude or ChatGPT what it needs before spending time writing a detailed prompt that misses key context.

title: Get sharper AI outputs with the Role-Context-Task-Format prompt structure
whatItDoes: A four-part prompt structure — Role, Context, Task, Format — that gives the AI clear signals instead of a vague request. The guide also covers six complementary techniques: Chain-of-Thought, Few-Shot, Constraint-Based, Iterative Refinement, Negative Prompting, and Meta-Prompting.
whatItImproves: Replaces open-ended prompts with a reliable structure that reduces hallucinations and back-and-forth, producing better-quality outputs in fewer attempts.
howToTry:
1. Open ChatGPT or Claude.
2. Structure your prompt with four parts: Role (who the AI should be), Context (the situation), Task (what to do), Format (how to present the output).
3. For reasoning tasks, add 'Think step by step' to trigger Chain-of-Thought.
4. For structured outputs, include 2–3 examples of your desired format (Few-Shot).
5. Iterate: refine the first response with a follow-up that adds constraints or addresses edge cases.
author: HonestAI

relevance.dailyImpact: When preparing a client status update or summarising a validation report, use Role+Context+Task+Format to get a formatted, audience-ready draft in one pass instead of multiple correction rounds.
relevance.practicalBenefit: Applying Few-Shot and Iterative Refinement to pharma document reviews lets you supply the AI with two examples of an acceptable summary or redaction, then harden the output with targeted follow-ups — cutting review cycles significantly.
relevance.whyRelevant: You regularly draft prompts for validation documents, client deliverables, and GxP-aware data tasks — a structured framework ensures the AI output matches the required tone, format, and accuracy standard on the first attempt.

title: Turn raw notes into a self-updating wiki — use voice dictation and agent skills to build a second brain
whatItDoes: A structured workflow that turns unorganized voice-dictated notes into a self-updating, browsable knowledge base. An /enrich-note agent skill stamps each note with tags, source URLs, and backlinks; a wiki skill compounds those notes into entity and concept pages; and scheduled automations keep everything refreshed — locally via Codex or in the cloud via a headless Obsidian sync.
whatItImproves: Before this workflow, raw notes stayed fragmented and unsearchable. After setting it up, agents maintain a compounding artefact — entity pages, topic syntheses, an index — rather than re-discovering your knowledge from scratch on every query, as with RAG-style retrieval.
howToTry:
1. Install the skills with npx skills add bholmesdev/llm-knowledge-base-skills and store all notes as markdown files in a raw/ directory.
2. Capture thoughts by voice dictation rather than typing — talking runs at 200 words a minute; tools like Voice Ink or Handy.computer work on-device with no subscription.
3. Run /enrich-note — the agent assigns tags from a fixed registry, researches source URLs, and adds backlinks to related notes via a Related section.
4. Run the wiki skill to generate a persistent, interlinked knowledge base from your enriched notes, seeded from Andrej Karpathy's llm-wiki gist.
5. Schedule /enrich-notes-loop and /refresh-wiki to run overnight — locally via Codex's Scheduled tab, or in the cloud via Oz connected to Obsidian Sync.
author: Ben Holmes

relevance.dailyImpact: After a client call or document review, you can dictate your observations on the way back to your desk and let the overnight enrichment cycle tag, link, and wiki-fy them — so your notes are structured and retrievable before you start work the next morning.
relevance.practicalBenefit: The resulting wiki gives agents a compounding knowledge base to draw from when drafting status updates, validation plan sections, or client-facing summaries, cutting the time spent re-briefing the AI on project context.
relevance.whyRelevant: When tracking evolving requirements and client feedback across multiple pharma projects, this workflow turns scattered voice notes and meeting rambles into a searchable, agent-navigable wiki — reducing the effort of re-explaining context at the start of every session.

title: Break a spec into ready-to-run tickets with /to-tickets — skip the manual issue-writing step
